aeo.what_is: Eating disorder with cycles of binge eating followed by purging or other behaviors to prevent weight gain.

content.description: Bulimia Nervosa (BN) is characterized by recurrent binge-eating episodes with a sense of loss of control followed by inappropriate compensatory behaviors (e.g., self-induced vomiting, laxatives/diuretics, fasting, excessive exercise). Self-evaluation is unduly influenced by body shape and weight. Individuals are typically normal weight or overweight, which can mask illness severity.
content.temporal_criteria: Both binge eating and compensatory behaviors must occur, on average, at least once weekly for 3 months. Episodes are considered 'recurrent' rather than isolated. The frequency determines severity: mild (1–3 per week), moderate (4–7), severe (8–13), extreme (14+). Remission requires absence of binge/purge behaviors for a specified period.
content.misdiagnosis_explained: Bulimia nervosa is often missed because individuals typically maintain normal weight, leading clinicians to overlook symptoms. Patients may hide purging due to shame and underreport behaviors. Dental problems or reflux may be treated without exploring eating patterns. It can be confused with binge eating disorder (which lacks regular compensatory behaviors), anorexia nervosa binge-purge type (which requires low weight), or simply chalked up to 'stress eating.' The core distinction is recurrent, out-of-control binges coupled with regular compensatory behaviors to prevent weight gain, along with overvaluation of weight and shape.
content.diagnostic_criteria: A. Recurrent binge eating (eating, in a discrete period, an amount definitely larger than most would eat, with loss of control). B. Recurrent inappropriate compensatory behaviors to prevent weight gain (vomiting, laxatives, diuretics, fasting, excessive exercise). C. Binge eating and compensatory behaviors occur, on average, at least once weekly for 3 months. D. Self-evaluation unduly influenced by body shape/weight. E. Not occurring exclusively during episodes of Anorexia Nervosa.
content.prevalence: Lifetime prevalence ~1–2% in females and lower in males; often underrecognized due to normal BMI.
content.age_of_onset: Typically late adolescence to early adulthood; can present in mid-life.
content.prognosis: Good response to evidence-based psychotherapy, especially CBT-E and fluoxetine. Early treatment and reduced purging frequency predict better outcomes. Risks include electrolyte abnormalities, GI complications, and mood/anxiety comorbidities.

circuitry: Hyper-responsivity of mesolimbic reward pathways (ventral striatum) to palatable food cues.
Reduced top-down control in prefrontal regions during cue exposure and negative affect.
Insula/interoceptive differences contributing to dysregulated satiety signals.
neurochemistry: Serotonergic dysregulation (implicated in satiety, mood, and impulse control).
Dopaminergic reward signaling alterations reinforcing binge-purge cycles.
Endogenous opioid system involvement during binge episodes.
neurobiology.genetic_environmental: Polygenic risk overlaps with mood/anxiety; weight stigma, chronic dieting, and adverse experiences elevate risk.

history_psychosocial: Frequency/timing of binges and compensatory behaviors; triggers (dietary restraint, negative affect, body dissatisfaction).
Dieting/weight cycling history; exercise patterns; substance use; suicidality/self-harm.
Psychiatric comorbidities (depression, anxiety, OCD), trauma history.
medical_assessment: Labs: CMP with electrolytes (potassium, bicarbonate), magnesium, phosphorus; CBC; urinalysis as indicated.
ECG if hypokalemia, chest pain, syncope, or stimulant/med use; consider amylase, salivary gland exam.
physical_signs: Parotid/salivary gland enlargement, dental enamel erosion, oral ulcers, pharyngitis.
Russell’s sign (dorsal hand calluses), conjunctival petechiae, GI complaints (reflux, constipation).
standardized_measures: PHQ-9, GAD-7 for mood/anxiety; CIA for impairment.
risk_stratification: Urgent referral/hospitalization for severe electrolyte disturbance (e.g., K+ <3.0 mmol/L), syncope, significant dehydration, hematemesis/esophageal injury, uncontrolled vomiting, suicidality, or inability to interrupt purging.
differential_diagnosis: Binge Eating Disorder (binges without regular compensatory behaviors).
Anorexia Nervosa, binge-eating/purging type (underweight/low weight trajectory).
GI disorders (e.g., cyclic vomiting) without weight/shape overvaluation.
Major depression with hyperphagia without discrete binges.
evaluation.team_and_process: Coordinate care among therapist (CBT-E/IPT), medical provider, dietitian; psychiatry for medication management. Dental referral for enamel care; GI consult if alarm symptoms.

behavioral: Recurrent binge eating with loss of control.
Self-induced vomiting, laxative/diuretic misuse, fasting, or excessive exercise.
Secretive eating and food hoarding; rigid food rules.
cognitive: All-or-nothing thinking about food and exercise.
physical: Sore throat, dental sensitivity, swollen glands, reflux.

biological: Female sex (any gender can be affected)
psychological: Body dissatisfaction and internalized weight bias

impact_on_life.home: Secrecy, conflict around food/finances, strained relationships.
impact_on_life.school_work: Impaired concentration, schedule disruptions due to binges/purging.
impact_on_life.social: Avoidance of shared meals; social withdrawal.
impact_on_life.medical: Electrolyte abnormalities, dental erosion, reflux, menstrual irregularities.

psychotherapy: CBT-E (first-line): regular eating, reduce dietary restraint, address overvaluation, relapse prevention.
Interpersonal Psychotherapy (IPT) as alternative first-line when CBT-E unavailable or patient preference.
DBT skills modules for emotion regulation and distress tolerance when affect-driven binges prominent.
Family-Based Treatment for BN (FBT-BN) for adolescents.
nutrition_rehabilitation: Dietitian-guided structured meals/snacks to normalize intake and reduce binge triggers.
Education on binge–restriction cycle; gradual exposure to avoided foods.
medical_management: Correct electrolytes and dehydration; monitor K+, Mg, phosphate until stable.
Dental care for enamel protection; treat reflux/GERD.
Avoid routine ipecac or emetic agents (toxic).
medications: Fluoxetine (SSRI) — FDA-approved for BN; often titrated to 60 mg/day for binge/purge reduction.
Other SSRIs (e.g., sertraline, citalopram) if fluoxetine not tolerated (off-label).
Topiramate may reduce binge/purge frequency but carries cognitive and kidney stone risks (off-label; specialist-guided).
Avoid bupropion due to seizure risk in eating disorders with purging.
lifestyle_interventions: Non-compensatory, health-focused physical activity when medically appropriate.
Coping plans for high-risk times/places (meal support, urge surfing, stimulus control).
care_coordination: Regular medical monitoring during early recovery; crisis plan for suicidality.
Collaborate with school/athletics regarding accommodations and return-to-play when indicated.

treatment_goals: Eliminate binge/purge behaviors and normalize eating patterns.
Reduce overvaluation of weight/shape and body checking/avoidance.
Stabilize mood/anxiety and improve coping with triggers.
Address medical/dental sequelae and restore social/role functioning.
Develop relapse-prevention plan with early warning sign monitoring.
missed_diagnosis_factors: Normal BMI leading clinicians to overlook symptoms.
Patient secrecy and shame; underreporting of purging or laxative use.
Attributing reflux/dental problems to unrelated causes without screening for purging.
Focus on depression/anxiety without eating-behavior assessment.
overdiagnosis_factors: Labeling occasional overeating with guilt as BN without objective binges and compensatory behaviors.
Diagnosing BN when binges occur without compensatory behaviors (suggests BED).
Misclassifying underweight individuals with binge/purge as BN instead of AN binge/purge type.

specifiers.purge_methods_note: Specify predominant compensatory behaviors (vomiting, laxatives, diuretics, fasting, excessive exercise) to guide medical monitoring.

warning_signs: Recurrent sore throat, dental sensitivity/erosion, swollen cheeks (parotid enlargement).
Lightheadedness, palpitations, or muscle cramps (possible electrolyte disturbances).
Frequent bathroom use after meals; hidden food wrappers or laxatives/diuretics.
self_help_strategies: Adopt a 3-meals + 2–3 snacks pattern to reduce extreme hunger.
Remove or limit access to binge/purge cues (stimulus control); eat with support when possible.
Practice urge delay (10–20 minutes) with alternative coping (grounding, paced breathing, reaching out).
Schedule regular therapy/medical follow-up; use crisis plan for high-risk urges.

adolescence: Binges often follow dieting or peer/athletics pressures; FBT-BN and CBT-E adapted for youth are effective.
young_adulthood: Academic/work stress and independence challenges; medication plus CBT-E common.
adulthood: Chronic patterns possible; focus on relapse prevention, medical/dental repair, and comorbidity management.

first_person_statements: The binge-purge cycle felt like a secret I couldn't escape. I'd promise myself 'never again,' then find myself doing it hours later.
I thought purging was the solution to my binge eating, but it actually made everything worse—I was more obsessed with food and my body than ever.
My teeth started to hurt and my throat was always sore, but I couldn't stop. I was so ashamed I didn't tell anyone for years.
Recovery taught me that the restriction was fueling the binges. When I started eating regularly, the urge to binge dropped dramatically.
I didn't realize how much the bulimia controlled my life until I got better. I can finally go out to dinner without planning how to purge afterward.
Learning to sit with uncomfortable feelings instead of using food and purging to cope was the hardest and most important part of recovery.

real_life_examples: A 17-year-old track athlete begins restrictive dieting before her season, cutting carbs and skipping breakfast. Within weeks, she starts experiencing intense hunger in the evenings and binges on large amounts of food her parents bought for the family. Feeling guilty and terrified of weight gain, she begins self-inducing vomiting every morning. Her parents notice she's frequently in the bathroom after meals and find hidden food wrappers. They bring her to her pediatrician, who refers her to an eating disorder specialist. Family-Based Treatment for Bulimia Nervosa (FBT-BN) helps her parents provide structured, regular meals and snacks, which reduces extreme hunger and binge urges. Within 4 weeks, purging stops, and over 3 months, she learns to eat flexibly without compensatory behaviors.

A 26-year-old woman with a history of depression starts binge eating after stressful workdays, consuming entire boxes of cookies, bags of chips, and takeout in one sitting. She feels intense shame and uses laxatives to 'undo' the binges, often taking 20–30 pills at a time. After experiencing severe abdominal cramping and rectal bleeding, she seeks medical help. Her doctor orders labs showing electrolyte imbalances and refers her to therapy. CBT-E addresses the restrict-binge-purge cycle, food rules, and overvaluation of shape/weight. Her psychiatrist prescribes fluoxetine (60 mg daily), which helps reduce binge/purge frequency and depressive symptoms. She also sees a dietitian to rebuild regular eating patterns and a dentist to address enamel erosion. After 6 months of treatment, she achieves full remission and maintains recovery with ongoing therapy and check-ins.

A 21-year-old college student has been binge eating and purging since age 16, initially triggered by dieting and weight-based teasing. She purges multiple times a day, often missing classes to buy binge foods or recover from exhaustion. Her grades suffer, and she becomes socially isolated. She faints during an exam due to dehydration and low potassium, prompting an ER visit. Hospitalization corrects her electrolytes, and she transitions to a partial hospitalization program (PHP) with daily therapy, meal support, and medical monitoring. In PHP, she participates in CBT-E groups, learns urge-surfing and distress tolerance skills, and works with a dietitian to normalize her eating. After 8 weeks of intensive treatment and a step-down to outpatient care, she returns to school with a strong relapse-prevention plan and weekly therapy.

A 34-year-old mother of two secretly binges and purges when her kids are asleep or at school. She spends hundreds of dollars monthly on binge foods, hides evidence, and feels increasing shame and isolation. Her husband notices dental damage and frequent nausea, and she finally discloses her bulimia after years of secrecy. She enters outpatient treatment with a therapist trained in CBT-E and begins fluoxetine. Her husband attends family sessions to learn how to support her without monitoring or commenting on her eating. She practices planned, balanced meals and uses coping skills (journaling, calling her therapist, going for walks) when urges arise. Over a year, binge/purge episodes decrease from daily to rare, and she rebuilds trust with her family and herself.

A 19-year-old male starts using vomiting to control his weight after being told by his wrestling coach to drop a weight class. What begins as occasional purging becomes a daily cycle of bingeing (triggered by severe restriction) and vomiting. He develops parotid gland swelling, frequent heartburn, and fatigue. When his coach notices his performance declining and he admits the purging, he's referred to a sports medicine physician who diagnoses bulimia nervosa. He takes a break from wrestling and starts CBT-E tailored to male athletes, focusing on regular eating, reducing overvaluation of weight, and managing competitive pressures. A dietitian helps him fuel appropriately for training. After treatment, he returns to wrestling with a healthier relationship to food and his body, competing at his natural weight.

comparisons.similarities: Both involve recurrent episodes of binge eating with a sense of loss of control, often triggered by restriction or negative emotions.
comparisons.differences: In bulimia nervosa, binges are regularly followed by compensatory behaviors (purging, fasting, excessive exercise) to prevent weight gain. In binge eating disorder, there are no regular compensatory behaviors. BED is also more common in individuals with higher body weight, whereas bulimia is typically at normal or slightly above-normal weight.

comparisons.similarities: Both can involve binge eating, purging (vomiting, laxatives), and overvaluation of weight and shape.
comparisons.differences: Anorexia nervosa requires significantly low body weight, while bulimia nervosa occurs at normal or higher weight. In anorexia, weight and shape concerns lead to severe restriction with or without binge/purge episodes, whereas bulimia centers on the binge-purge cycle without sustained low weight.

comparisons.similarities: Both may involve regurgitation of food.
comparisons.differences: In rumination disorder, regurgitation is effortless, often re-chewed and re-swallowed or spit out, without the intent to prevent weight gain. It lacks the binge eating, distress about body shape/weight, and intentional purging that characterize bulimia nervosa.

comparisons.similarities: Both can involve increased eating and emotional distress.
comparisons.differences: In depression, eating may increase as comfort or due to neurovegetative symptoms, but without the discrete, out-of-control binges and compensatory behaviors of bulimia. Bulimia's core feature is the binge-purge cycle driven by overvaluation of weight/shape, not just mood-related appetite changes.

faqs.question: Is bulimia nervosa as serious as anorexia nervosa?
faqs.answer: Yes. Although people with bulimia are typically normal weight, the disorder carries serious medical risks, including life-threatening electrolyte imbalances, cardiac arrhythmias, esophageal rupture, and dental damage. Both conditions require specialized treatment and can be fatal without intervention.

faqs.question: Can you have bulimia if you don't vomit?
faqs.answer: Yes. Purging can include self-induced vomiting, but also misuse of laxatives, diuretics, or enemas. Non-purging compensatory behaviors like fasting or excessive exercise also count. If binge eating is followed by any regular compensatory behavior to prevent weight gain, it may be bulimia nervosa.

faqs.question: How do I know if I'm binge eating or just overeating?
faqs.answer: A binge involves eating an objectively large amount of food in a discrete period (e.g., within 2 hours) with a sense of loss of control—feeling unable to stop or regulate how much you eat. Occasional overeating (like at holiday meals) without loss of control is not binge eating.

faqs.question: Will I gain a lot of weight if I stop purging?
faqs.answer: Most people maintain or experience modest weight changes when they stop purging and normalize eating. Purging is ineffective at preventing weight gain long-term and often leads to more bingeing due to physical and psychological deprivation. Regular, balanced eating stabilizes weight more effectively than the binge-purge cycle.

faqs.question: Why can't I just stop bingeing?
faqs.answer: Binge eating is often driven by restriction (dieting, skipping meals), emotional triggers, or ingrained habits. It's reinforced by brain reward pathways and relieved temporarily by purging, creating a hard-to-break cycle. Treatment helps identify triggers, normalize eating, and develop healthier coping skills so you can stop bingeing without willpower alone.

faqs.question: Is fluoxetine the only medication for bulimia?
faqs.answer: Fluoxetine (Prozac) is the only FDA-approved medication for bulimia nervosa, typically prescribed at 60 mg/day. Other SSRIs (sertraline, citalopram) may also reduce binge/purge frequency. Topiramate is sometimes used off-label. However, medication works best when combined with therapy like CBT-E, not as a standalone treatment.

faqs.question: Can bulimia nervosa cause permanent damage?
faqs.answer: Some effects, like dental enamel erosion, esophageal damage, and bone density loss, may be lasting, especially if illness is chronic. However, many complications improve with treatment: electrolyte levels normalize, GI symptoms resolve, and menstrual cycles return. Early treatment minimizes long-term harm.

faqs.question: Do laxatives actually help lose weight or prevent absorption?
faqs.answer: No. Laxatives work on the large intestine after calories have already been absorbed in the small intestine. The weight loss from laxatives is water and electrolyte loss, which is temporary and dangerous. Laxative misuse can cause dehydration, electrolyte imbalances, and lasting damage to bowel function.

faqs.question: What is CBT-E and how does it help bulimia?
faqs.answer: CBT-E (Enhanced Cognitive Behavioral Therapy) is the gold-standard psychotherapy for bulimia nervosa. It addresses the thoughts and behaviors that maintain the disorder: dietary restraint, overvaluation of shape/weight, binge triggers, and mood regulation. Over 16–20 sessions, CBT-E helps you establish regular eating, reduce binge/purge behaviors, and prevent relapse.

faqs.question: How long does recovery from bulimia nervosa take?
faqs.answer: It varies. Some people achieve remission in a few months with outpatient CBT-E and medication, while others need longer or more intensive treatment (e.g., partial hospitalization). Early engagement, reducing dietary restraint, regular eating, and strong support improve speed of recovery. Relapse prevention work continues even after symptoms resolve.

faqs.question: Can you recover from bulimia on your own?
faqs.answer: While some individuals may reduce symptoms, professional treatment significantly improves outcomes and addresses underlying factors. Evidence-based therapy (CBT-E or IPT), medical monitoring, nutritional counseling, and sometimes medication are key to full, lasting recovery. Self-help resources can supplement treatment but are rarely sufficient alone.

faqs.question: Why do I feel so tired and foggy with bulimia?
faqs.answer: Binge-purge cycles disrupt your body's electrolytes (potassium, sodium, magnesium), leading to fatigue, weakness, and difficulty concentrating. Dehydration, nutritional deficiencies, and irregular eating patterns also impair energy and cognition. These symptoms improve as eating normalizes and purging stops.

faqs.question: Can stress cause bulimia nervosa?
faqs.answer: Stress doesn't directly cause bulimia, but it's a common trigger for binge eating and can worsen symptoms. People with bulimia often use binge/purge behaviors to cope with negative emotions, anxiety, or overwhelming situations. Treatment teaches healthier emotion regulation strategies to replace the binge-purge cycle.

faqs.question: Is it safe to exercise if I have bulimia?
faqs.answer: If you're medically stable (normal electrolytes, hydration, and heart function), moderate exercise is generally safe. However, if exercise is used as a compensatory behavior (excessively or compulsively to 'burn off' calories), it's part of the disorder and should be addressed in treatment. Your medical team will guide safe activity levels.

faqs.question: What should I do if I relapse after treatment?
faqs.answer: Relapse is common, especially during stress or life transitions, but it doesn't mean treatment failed. Reach out to your therapist or treatment team immediately. Early intervention can prevent a full relapse. Use your relapse-prevention plan: return to regular eating, identify triggers, and resume coping skills and support.

faqs.question: Can males have bulimia nervosa?
faqs.answer: Yes. Bulimia affects people of all genders, though it's more common in females. Males may be underdiagnosed due to stigma and misconceptions about eating disorders. Symptoms, risks, and treatments are similar across genders.

faqs.question: How do I tell my family or friends I have bulimia?
faqs.answer: Choose a private, calm moment and be honest: 'I've been struggling with binge eating and purging, and I need help.' Share as much as you're comfortable with and let them know how they can support you (e.g., not commenting on your eating, helping you get treatment). It's okay to bring a therapist or written statement if that feels easier.

faqs.question: Will my teeth recover after I stop purging?
faqs.answer: Enamel erosion is not reversible, but further damage can be prevented by stopping purging. A dentist can provide treatments like fluoride varnish, bonding, or crowns to protect and repair teeth. Rinsing with water (not brushing immediately) after vomiting reduces acid exposure if purging hasn't stopped yet.

content.when_to_seek_help: Seek urgent medical care for fainting, chest pain, vomiting blood, or severe weakness. Arrange specialized eating-disorder evaluation if binge/purge behaviors occur weekly, or if there are dental/GI complications, electrolyte abnormalities, or significant distress.

positive_factors: Early engagement in CBT-E or FBT-BN
Reduction of dietary restraint and regular eating
challenging_factors: High frequency of purging or laxative misuse
Severe comorbid depression/anxiety or substance use
Long duration of untreated illness and high weight/shape overvaluation

tiles.title: What is Bulimia Nervosa?
tiles.summary: Recurrent binge eating followed by purging or other compensatory behaviors to prevent weight gain.

tiles.title: Signs & Symptoms
tiles.summary: Loss-of-control eating episodes, self-induced vomiting, laxative use, dental damage, and swollen glands.

tiles.title: Causes & Risk Factors
tiles.summary: Genetic vulnerability, dieting culture, perfectionism, impulsivity, weight stigma, and chronic stress.

tiles.title: How It's Diagnosed
tiles.summary: Clinical interview about binge/purge patterns, medical exam, lab work, and eating disorder assessments.

tiles.title: Treatment Options
tiles.summary: CBT-E, Interpersonal Psychotherapy, fluoxetine, nutritional counseling, and medical monitoring.

tiles.title: Medical Complications
tiles.summary: Electrolyte imbalances, cardiac arrhythmias, esophageal damage, dental erosion, and GI issues.

tiles.title: Recovery & Prognosis
tiles.summary: Good response to therapy and medication. Early treatment reduces binge/purge frequency and improves outcomes.

tiles.title: Living with Bulimia
tiles.summary: Regular structured eating, reducing dietary restraint, managing triggers, and maintaining treatment support.

tiles.title: Getting Help
tiles.summary: Seek specialized eating disorder care for recurrent binge/purge behaviors or medical complications.
